protections: A stored partial pipeline may be resumed only by the client session that created it: the resume token presented in the request must be bound to the token recorded in that session, not merely be a valid token for the same backend (social_core/utils.py:185-216).

An intentional out-of-band resume (the emailed email-validation link opened in a fresh session) must keep working, and the allowance is recorded on that step's stored partial only rather than granted blanket (social_core/pipeline/mail.py:13-37, social_core/pipeline/partial.py:8-59).

The ownership decision is applied at every resume sink (public utility, both framework actions, and backend continue_pipeline overrides), not only in the login action (social_core/actions.py:96-100, social_core/actions.py:176-182, social_core/backends/base.py:269-275, social_core/backends/open_id.py:189-200).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: The partial_token is an unguessable uuid4 capability (social_core/storage.py:421-422) and resuming a pipeline from a token is the documented public contract of this utility, so a request-supplied token looks like an already-authenticated capability rather than user-controlled input.

do_disconnect is reached only with an already-authenticated user and the advisory describes the login/complete flow, so the disconnect caller looks out of scope and a fix written inside do_complete alone appears sufficient.

Framework views are expected to pass the token in request data, so the explicit partial_token argument and the configurable PARTIAL_PIPELINE_TOKEN_NAME name look like internal/rare shapes that a check on request_data['partial_token'] need not cover.

mail_validation is applied with the plain @partial alias and already checks the verification_code (mail.py:23-29), so the emailed token looks like a self-authenticating exception and the step's cross-session resume policy looks like an internal decorator detail.

The store path is an internal decorator/serializer concern (the decorator already calls partial_prepare), so where the resume-policy flag is written looks like an implementation detail and a flag placed in the ordinary kwargs appears to be persisted and restored like every other value.

BaseStrategy hosts framework extension points whose base behaviour is commonly a permissive no-op (as openid_session_dict or partial_load are), so the default of a new external-resume confirmation hook looks like it cannot itself be the security decision.

partial_load(token) plus continue_pipeline(partial) is a lower-level library API used by framework integrations and by the project's own test harness, not a user-facing web route, so the advisory's complete/disconnect handlers can be argued to be the whole scope.

BaseOpenID is a legacy OpenID 2.0 backend with its own continue_pipeline override, and the HTTP path still passes through the guard upstream in partial_pipeline_data, so the override looks like a neighbouring/legacy path rather than a second resume implementation.

masking: The email-validation resume currently works only because T1's hole exists; adding the session-ownership check without T4/T5's recorded allowance turns that flow into a regression rather than keeping it alive.

T2 and T3 only become visible once the guard is written at the shared utility; a guard placed in do_complete alone hides them until the disconnect path or an explicit partial_token argument is exercised.

conflicts.what: Requiring the resume token to equal the session token (T1) refuses the emailed validation link opened in a fresh session, which mail_validation depends on because it puts the same token in the email (mail.py:30-33); the flow survives only if the allowance is recorded per stored partial and confirmed before the check denies.

A check written only against request_data['partial_token'] passes the common case but leaves the explicit partial_token argument and a renamed PARTIAL_PIPELINE_TOKEN_NAME resolving to the stored partial unchecked, so the natural fix for T1 does not close T3 unless the check applies to the resolved token.

fairness_risks: Email-validation links are a legitimate cross-session resume: mail_validation sends current_partial.token to the user's address (pipeline/mail.py:30-33) and the link is expected to work in a different browser or after the session expired; any rule that refuses a request token not present in the session contradicts this supported flow (strategy.py:163-174, 176-185).

partial_step(save_to_session=False) deliberately records no session token (pipeline/partial.py:8, 45-50; exercised at tests/test_partial.py:58), so a rule of 'no session token means refuse' rejects a supported decorator shape.

Framework views may pass partial_token as an explicit argument (utils.py:185-186) or configure PARTIAL_PIPELINE_TOKEN_NAME (utils.py:182-184); refusing all request-supplied tokens breaks stateless/mobile integrations that legitimately resume from a token.

The repository's own partial-pipeline tests pop PARTIAL_TOKEN_SESSION_NAME before resuming: tests/backends/base.py:155-159 and 166-170, tests/test_pipeline.py:221-224 and 245-248. A guard placed in strategy.partial_load or BaseAuth.continue_pipeline (T7) or in the OpenID override (T8) makes those tests fail, so those two traps can only be graded if the hidden suite drops or rewrites them.

The session holds only the most recent token (pipeline/partial.py:48-50 overwrites it each time a step halts), so an exact-equality rule can refuse a legitimate resume of an older in-flight partial in a second tab.

partial_pipeline_data is a public utility used by third-party framework strategies; changing its contract to require a session match is a breaking change for callers that legitimately resume from a token (utils.py:173-179).

design.why: Four independent groups with genuinely different reasons to dismiss, mixing deepseek- and mimo-type mechanisms: T1 is the absent check at the landing point with a capability-token argument for leaving it alone; T4 is the coupled must-keep-working email link that a blanket fix breaks (mimo); T7 is the unguarded loader/continue_pipeline sink argued away as a library API; T8 is the BaseOpenID override argued away as legacy. T2 and T3 add the parallel caller and the resolved-token shape inside T1's group without adding a new dismissal reason, and T5/T6 add the producer and default-value failure modes inside T4's group. This beats a T1-only or T1+T4 design because it forces three separate ownership-boundary judgements (where the check lives, what may still resume out of band, whether the lower-level sink needs its own guard) instead of one edit to partial_pipeline_data. Caveat: T7 and T8 are only gradeable if the hidden suite does not retain the repo's existing resume-after-session_pop tests (tests/backends/base.py:155-170, tests/test_pipeline.py:221-248); if it does, the fair stack reduces to T1+T4 and this candidate falls below the 3-trap bar.
